title: Where is the chain after two steps?

prereqs.why: The distribution after n steps is the initial row vector times the nth power of the transition matrix.
That the matrix can be applied twice at all is the Markov property plus time homogeneity.

statement:
A Markov chain on $S = \{1,2,3\}$ has transition matrix

$$P = \begin{pmatrix}
\tfrac12 & \tfrac12 & 0\\[2pt]
0 & \tfrac12 & \tfrac12\\[2pt]
\tfrac12 & 0 & \tfrac12
\end{pmatrix}$$

where the entry in row $i$ and column $j$ is $p_{i,j} = \P(X_{n+1} = j \mid X_n = i)$.

The initial distribution is $\lambda^{(0)} = \bigl(\tfrac12, \tfrac12, 0\bigr)$.

Give $\P(X_2 = 2)$ exactly.
hints: The distribution after $n$ steps is $\lambda^{(0)} P^n$, a row vector times a matrix — so you multiply on the left.
Do it in two steps rather than squaring the matrix: compute $\lambda^{(1)} = \lambda^{(0)} P$ first, and check that its entries sum to 1.
$\lambda^{(1)} = (1/4, 1/2, 1/4)$. Now take its product with the **second column** of $P$.

payload.prompt: The probability of being in state 2 at time 2.
payload.label: $\P(X_2 = 2) =$
payload.syntax: A number or a fraction. Arithmetic is fine.
